title: Data Structures
tagline: Stacks, queues, infix-to-prefix/postfix, singly linked lists and binary trees, with structure-selection reasoning.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material for the CISCE ISC Class XII Computer Science syllabus (subject code 868), examination year 2027, Section C. The syllabus topic list was taken from the verified 2027 syllabus; the explanations, examples and questions here are original and were not taken from any board examination paper, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Data structures are ways of organising related values so that common operations become easy or hard. This chapter covers the structures named in Section C of the 2027 syllabus: stacks, queues, circular queues and dequeue, infix-to-prefix and infix-to-postfix conversion, singly linked lists, and conceptual binary trees. The aim is not just to define each structure, but to understand what each one makes easy, what it makes awkward, and how to choose among them.

learn.title: Why data structures matter in this syllabus

blocks.text: A data structure is a way of organising related values so that common operations are easy or hard to do. The syllabus does not assume that you will learn a big library of advanced data structures. Instead, it focuses on a small set of structures that show up repeatedly in computer science and in examination questions: stacks, queues, linked lists and binary trees. The point of this section is not just to know the definitions, but to understand when each structure is a sensible choice and when it is not.

When you choose a structure, you are choosing which operations will be convenient and which will be expensive. A stack is convenient for the last-in-first-out order that matches nested processing; a queue is convenient for first-come-first-served waiting lines; a linked list is convenient when items are inserted or removed frequently in the middle; a binary tree is convenient when the data has a natural hierarchy. The examination often asks students to decide which structure fits a given situation rather than simply to recite definitions. That decision-making is what this chapter builds toward.

items: A data structure is a way of organising related values and the operations that work on them.
Different structures make different operations convenient.
Choosing a structure is a design decision about what order and access patterns matter.
The syllabus focuses on stacks, queues, singly linked lists and binary trees.
The examination often tests selection of a structure to match a real situation.

blocks.text: A stack is a structure that lets you add and remove values only from one end, the top. The last value added is the first value removed, which is why a stack is described as LIFO. The two basic operations are push, which adds a value to the top, and pop, which removes the top value. You can also peek at the top value without removing it. A stack is empty when there are no values on it, and trying to pop from an empty stack is an error called underflow. If the stack has a fixed capacity and you push when it is already full, you get overflow.

The stack idea shows up naturally wherever processing is nested. A browser history of back buttons, the order of method calls during execution, the matching of brackets in an expression, and the evaluation of postfix expressions all behave like stacks. That is why the syllabus associates stacks with bracket matching and postfix evaluation. The key property is not the physical metaphor but the access order: the most recently added item is the one you deal with next.

items.text: Push A, then B, then C onto an empty stack.
items.note: The top is now C. Popping gives C, then B, then A.
Scan a bracket expression left to right; push opening brackets, pop and compare when you see a closing bracket. If the stack ends empty and every close matched, the brackets are balanced.
Scan a postfix expression; when you see a number push it, when you see an operator pop the required operands, apply the operator and push the result.

blocks.text: A queue is a structure that adds values at one end, the rear, and removes them from the other end, the front. The first value added is the first value removed, which is why a queue is described as FIFO. The basic operations are enqueue, which adds a value to the rear, and dequeue, which removes the value at the front. People often think of a queue as a waiting line: the person who arrives first is served first, and new arrivals join the back of the line. That metaphor matches the abstract structure exactly.

A simple array-based queue has a problem called false overflow. As values are dequeued from the front, the front index moves forward, and eventually the rear can no longer advance even though there is empty space earlier in the array. A circular queue avoids this by letting the rear wrap around to the beginning of the array when it reaches the end. The same idea applies to the front as values are removed. Distinguishing a linear queue from a circular queue is a standard part of the syllabus, and the examination often asks why a circular arrangement is used.

A dequeue, also called a double-ended queue, extends the queue idea by allowing insertion and removal at both ends. That makes it more flexible than a simple FIFO queue, because you can add or remove from either side. The syllabus mentions dequeue alongside circular queue, and students should be able to describe what extra flexibility a dequeue provides.

items.note: Front is 1, rear is 3. Dequeue gives 1, then 2, then 3.

items.text: False overflow in a linear queue.
items.note: If items keep being dequeued from the front and enqueued at the rear of a fixed array, the rear may hit the end while empty slots remain near the front.
By wrapping the indices around the array, a circular queue can keep using the same array until it is genuinely full.

learn.title: Infix, prefix and postfix, and why stacks help

blocks.text: Expressions can be written in several notations. In infix notation, the operator sits between its operands, as in A + B. In prefix notation, the operator sits before its operands, as in + A B. In postfix notation, also called reverse Polish notation, the operator sits after its operands, as in A B +. Each notation has advantages. Infix is familiar to people, but it needs parentheses or precedence rules to remove ambiguity. Postfix has no ambiguity and is easy to evaluate with a stack, which is why postfix evaluation is a classic stack application in the syllabus.

Converting infix to postfix with a stack is one of the more examination-frequent tasks. The idea is to read the infix expression, output operands immediately, and use a stack to hold operators until their operands are ready. Precedence and parentheses decide when an operator leaves the stack. The same general idea works in reverse for infix-to-prefix conversion, and the stack remains the central tool because the conversion has to remember operators whose operands are not yet complete. Students do not need to memorize a long procedure as if it were a recipe; they need to understand that the stack preserves pending operators in the correct order.

items.text: Infix A + B becomes postfix A B +.
items.note: The operands A and B stay in order; the operator moves to the right.

items.text: Infix A + B * C becomes postfix A B C * +.
items.note: The multiplication has higher precedence, so its operator appears before the addition operator in postfix.

items.text: Postfix A B + C * means (A + B) * C.
items.note: In postfix the order of evaluation follows the operands and operators without parentheses.

items: Infix places the operator between operands; prefix places it before; postfix places it after.

learn.title: Singly linked lists: a chain of nodes

blocks.text: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes, where each node holds a value and a link to the next node. The first node is called the head. The last node usually has a null link, meaning there is no next node. Unlike an array, a linked list does not store its elements in consecutive memory and does not have to move elements around when you insert or delete in the middle. That makes linked lists attractive when you expect frequent insertions and deletions, especially at positions other than the two ends.

The cost of that flexibility is that you cannot jump directly to the middle of a linked list by index. To reach the third node, you must start at the head and follow three links. That is why linked lists are good for some things and poor for others. The syllabus expects students to know the basic operations: create a node, insert a node, delete a node, traverse the list, check whether it is empty, and in some cases reverse the list or work with a sublist. The practical point is that each of these operations must follow links carefully so that no node is lost or pointed to twice by mistake.

items.note: Head points to the node holding 10, which points to 20, which points to 30, which points to null.
Create a new node whose next points to the current head, then make the head point to the new node. This is cheap and does not require traversing.

items.text: Delete a node in the middle.
items.note: You must find the node before the one you want to delete, then change its next to skip the removed node. Otherwise the chain breaks.

blocks.text: A binary tree is a hierarchical structure made of nodes, where each node has at most two children, usually called the left child and the right child. One node is the root. The root is the starting point for the whole tree, and every other node is reachable from the root by following child links downward. A node with no children is called a leaf. The depth or level of a node is how far it is from the root, and the height of a tree is a measure of how tall it is, often defined in terms of the longest path from the root to a leaf.

The syllabus treats binary trees at a conceptual level for this syllabus. That means students should be able to talk about the parts of a tree, describe common terms such as root, leaf, subtree, sibling, parent, height, depth, level and size, and understand why a binary tree is useful when data has a natural hierarchy. Traversal is the usual way to visit every node in a tree. The common traversals are inorder, preorder and postorder, and each visits nodes in a different order. Students should be able to explain what each traversal does and what kind of situation it suits.

Binary trees also connect to the idea of balancing and completeness. A complete binary tree packs nodes neatly, level by level, and a balanced tree keeps the height small so that operations stay efficient. These ideas are conceptual here rather than algorithmic, but they matter because they explain why the shape of a tree affects its usefulness. The examination is more likely to ask for definitions, traversals and structure-selection reasoning than to require a full implementation of self-balancing trees.

learn.title: Choosing a structure: what the syllabus wants you to reason about

blocks.text: A recurring theme in this part of the syllabus is not just knowing each structure but choosing among them. A stack is the right choice when you need last-in-first-out behaviour or nested processing. A queue is the right choice when you need first-come-first-served order. A linked list is the right choice when insertions and deletions are frequent and you do not need fast access by position. A binary tree is the right choice when the data has a hierarchy and you want to reflect that hierarchy in the structure. These decisions are about the shape of the problem, not about memorising one correct answer for every case.

The examination often presents a situation and asks which structure fits best, or asks why one structure would be awkward for a given task. For example, a queue is awkward if you need to remove the most recently added item, because a queue gives you the oldest item, not the newest. A stack is awkward if you need to process items in arrival order. A linked list is awkward if you need repeated fast access by index. A binary tree is awkward if there is no natural hierarchy. Learning to state the mismatch is part of the skill the syllabus is building.
